title: US state-by-state PKU market & coverage
source_note: Coverage-mandate facts are anchored to the most recent comprehensive state-by-state survey: the Catalyst Center (Boston University School of Public Health / ACMG-HRSA), 'State Statutes & Regulations on Dietary Treatment of Disorders Identified Through Newborn Screening,' Nov 2016 (35 states + jurisdictions have a private-insurance medical-food mandate; 16 have none), cross-checked against the National PKU News / NUCDF 'State Laws and Policies for the Coverage of Metabolic Food and Formula' table and NPKUA's insurance-coverage resources. THREE market caveats apply everywhere: (1) ERISA-exempt self-funded employer plans are not bound by any state mandate, so many privately-insured families still pay out of pocket; (2) mandates that cover 'formula only' leave low-protein modified foods (MLPFs) uncovered; (3) statutes change - confirm current text before relying on it. PKU population figures are scaled estimates (US affected population ~16,500, i.e. roughly 1 in 20,000 residents from a birth incidence of ~1 in 10,000-15,000), apportioned by 2023 state population; true counts vary with ancestry mix and are not registry-confirmed.

records.coverage_summary: No private-insurance mandate for PKU medical foods. Coverage runs through Medicaid (enteral, case-by-case), WIC, and Title V (Children's Rehabilitation Services; UAB Sparks Clinic).
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers metabolic foods case-by-case with age limits (Nutritional Product Grid); enteral emphasized.
records.clinics_note: UAB / Sparks Clinic at Children's of Alabama (Birmingham) metabolic program.
records.market_signal: Market gap: no mandate, so privately-insured families lean on patchy state programs and pay OOP for low-protein foods.

records.medicaid_note: Medicaid/EPSDT covers PKU formula for enrollees under 21 at high nutritional risk.
records.clinics_note: No in-state metabolic clinic; patients typically referred to Seattle Children's / OHSU.
records.market_signal: Formula-only, PKU-only mandate: families pay OOP for low-protein foods; remote geography compounds access cost.

records.medicaid_note: AHCCCS/Medicaid covers metabolic foods for NBS conditions incl PKU; WIC limited.

records.coverage_summary: Mandate (31A-22-623; R590-76-4 HMOs; R590-194) covers inborn errors of amino-acid or urea-cycle metabolism treatable by dietary restriction: dietary products (deductible/copay apply on major medical).
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers medical foods meeting the Orphan Drug Act definition (oral/tube) under 21, case-by-case.
records.clinics_note: University of Utah / Intermountain Primary Children's Hospital (Salt Lake City).
records.market_signal: Mandated but deductible/copay and case-by-case Medicaid create moderate OOP; ERISA exemption applies.

records.coverage_summary: Mandate (8 V.S.A. 4089e) covers inherited metabolic disease for all NBS conditions: medically necessary medical foods and low-protein modified food products; $2,500 cap on low-protein foods.
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers low-protein modified foods (Act 128); Title V CSHCN is payer of last resort.
records.clinics_note: University of Vermont Medical Center (Burlington).
records.market_signal: Broadly covered incl MLPFs; the $2,500 food cap and ERISA exemption are the residual gaps.

records.coverage_summary: No current private-insurance mandate in the 2016 survey (an earlier formula/food statute existed with a $2,000 cap and age limits; confirm current law). Coverage via Medicaid (tube feeding only) and Dept of Health (metabolic formula, low-protein food, supplements) under 21 / income-tested.
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers core NBS panel, tube feeding only; DOH program income-tested (under 21; over 21 if income <300% FPL; $1,500 cap above that).
records.clinics_note: Virginia Commonwealth University (Richmond), UVA (Charlottesville); Northern VA families use Children's National.
records.market_signal: Market gap: no active mandate per 2016 survey; tube-feeding-only Medicaid and income-tested DOH leave OOP for oral foods.

records.coverage_summary: Mandate (48.20.520; 48.21.300) covers PKU only (plus elemental formula for eosinophilic GI disorders): formula and medically necessary elemental formula - no broad low-protein-food benefit.
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid (WAC 388-554-300) covers oral/tube enteral nutrition products and supplies; specialty clinics cover NBS disorders.
records.clinics_note: Seattle Children's Hospital / University of Washington biochemical genetics.
records.market_signal: Partial: PKU-only mandate; non-PKU IEMs and low-protein foods depend on Medicaid/specialty clinics.

sources.title: State Statutes & Regulations on Dietary Treatment (Catalyst Center, BU), Nov 2016

records.coverage_summary: No private-insurance mandate. Coverage via Medicaid (formula only for PKU/GALT; must refer to WVU Genetics), WIC, and the Office of Maternal, Child & Family Health (metabolic formula/supplements for PKU, tyrosinemia, organic acidemias).
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers formula only, referred through the WVU Genetics team.
records.clinics_note: WVU Genetics team (Morgantown) is the state's central metabolic referral.
records.market_signal: Market gap: no mandate, formula-only Medicaid; low-protein foods largely OOP.

sources.title: State Statutes & Regulations on Dietary Treatment (Catalyst Center, BU), Nov 2016

records.coverage_summary: No private-insurance mandate. Coverage via Medicaid (HFS 107.09) for medically necessary specially formulated nutritional supplements and replacement products (enteral/parenteral) for nutritional risk; WIC shows no coverage in the survey.
records.medicaid_note: Medicaid covers medically necessary nutritional supplements/replacements incl metabolic disorders.
records.clinics_note: Children's Wisconsin / Medical College of Wisconsin (Milwaukee); UW-Madison.
records.market_signal: Market gap: no mandate; coverage rests on Medicaid medical-necessity, so many families pay OOP.

sources.title: State Statutes & Regulations on Dietary Treatment (Catalyst Center, BU), Nov 2016

records.coverage_summary: Mandate (26-20-401) covers a broad inherited-enzymatic-disorder list (PKU, maternal PKU, MSUD, TYR, HCY, urea-cycle disorders, GA, MMA, PROP, etc.): medical nutrition therapy. Medicaid and CSHCN add specialty formulas and medical foods.
records.medicaid_note: Wyoming Medicaid covers specialty formulas and medical foods for diagnosed IEM (amino/carb/fat) with treatment plan.
records.clinics_note: No in-state metabolic clinic; patients typically referred to Children's Hospital Colorado (Denver).
records.market_signal: Broad mandate on paper, but no in-state clinic means travel costs; ERISA exemption applies.
